Washington, July 1 (4)—Presi- 
dent Truman today signed legisla-

member of the International Refu- 
gee anization, saying the IRO 
willgive Id ‘‘new reason to 
believe. that no problem. is too dif- 
ficult” for solution by co-operating 
nations. 

Mr. Truman said he was “happy 
to accept membership” on behalf 
of this country as he signed the 
measure at a White House cere- 
mony. The agency will operate 
through the United Nations. 

Authorizes $73,500,000 

Besides providing for United 
States participation in the IRO, the 
legislation authorizes a $73,500,000 
contribution toward the care of 
Europe's 900,000 displaced persons 
in the next twelve months. . 

Mr. Truman also signed the 
necessary membership papers for. 
deposit with Trygve Lie, secretary. 
‘general gf the United Nations, by

uve to the United Na-

ment:

Girl Had Change

icago,, July 1 (4)—Rosanna 
everi, the English girl who balke¢

hat her final decision in her inte?

Rosanna, 24, traveled from Lon 
don alone,. against her parents 

ishes, she said, to wed, Vasque 

6-year-old express company work 
er. But the trip to-the altar iast 
Sunday gave her qualms. In the 
oe of the ceremony she said 
“ 0.” 

Marriage Off 

That decided Peter. The mar 
riage was off, he said, since “If 
she’s not certain, it wouldn’t be a 
good idea.” Then Rosanna exer- 
cised her woman’s prerogative 
again. She decided she wanted to 
go through with it after all. 

But Peter left his parents’ home, 
where Rosanna was staying, to live 
with friends. After a day’s thinking 
it over, Rosanna made her nega 
tive decision, which she said was 
her final one. 

“T’'ve just gotten to feel that he’s 
not really worth worrying about,” 
she declared. 


Will Not Return 

Asked if she would return to 
Giovanni Castellani, the man she 
left behind in London, Rosanna 
said, “It wouldn’t be right to marry 
someone you didn’t love.” 

Castellani told London newsmen 
he had been engaged to Rosanna 
when she left England for the} 
United States, and that he would 
be “happy to forget the past” if 
she would return to him. He is 
assistant manager of the cafe where 
Rosanna formerly worked as a 
waitress. 

Like A Brother 

But Rosanna described her “en- 
gagement” to Castellani as “just 
unofficial.” 

“He was more like ‘a brother to 
me,” she said. 

The young English girl said to- 
day she would like to spend a few. 
more days in Chicago, sightseeing, 
and then planned to go to liye 
with her mother’s sister, Mrs. Ida 
Mastrola, in Jersey City, N.J. She 
is attempting to arrange with the 
British consulate for an indefinite 
stay. in the United States, and 
hopes to obtain employment ‘doing 
embroidery and hand needlework. 

“I don’t intend to go back to 
England,” she_ said.

Communist Attempt 
‘Political Blackmail’ 
Chicago, July 1 (#)—Louis F. 


Budenz..former editor of the Daily 
Worker, official Communist news- 


‘} paper, said today the Communists 
dare threatening the Truman Ad- 


ministration with a third party as 
“political blackmail.” 

Addressing the Kiwanis Inter- 
national convention, Budénz said 
that a statement in the June issue 
of Political Affairs, which he des- 
cribes as “the official theoretical 
organ of the Comntunist party in 
America,” proclaims “virtual war- 
fare against the American nation.” 

“The third party movement in 
Communist hands is a piece of poli- 
tical blackmail direeted at the pres- 
ent administration in the hope that} 
this will compel a continuance of 
appeasement of Soviet Russia,” 
Budenz said. 

He said the June issue of Politi- 
cal Affairs stated that “American 
imperialism is seeking to Hitlerize 
the world.” 

Calls Party A Fifth Column 

“To every trained Communist 
that term is clear,” Budenz con- 
tinued. “It means that the United 
States must be fought to the bitter 
end, and by every means at the dis- 
posal of the Communist conspiracy. 

“To carry on this warfare against 
he American republic, the Com- 
munists further declare ... that 
hey will conduct within our coun- 
ry a battle for a people’s peace. 
But what, pray, is a people’s peace? 
It is the peace, they declare, de- 
sired by the Soviet dictatorship! 
It is a peace, then, in which the 
slave state is extended by con- 
inued aggressions, as we witness 
is the case.” 

Budenz said the Communist 
party in the United States was “a 
fifth column, having no right on 
American soil, totally alien to 
American life.”

Hits at Other ‘Faults’ 


Molotov, besides charging that 
the British-French plan would 
threaten ‘the sovereignty of some 
countries, struck out at two other 
faults which he said the plan con- 
tained. 

The first, he said, was that Bri- 
tain and France wold form a do- 
minant group within the proposed 
committee. 

The second was'that no attempt 
had been made to set up an all- 
German government, that even fur- 
ther divisions of western Germany 
were being contemplated, and that 
in proposing to use German repar- 
ations “for purposes other than re- 
parations” the plan showed “no spe- 
cial concern for those countries 
which had made the greatest sac- |

PARIS, July 2 (AP)—Following 
is the text of Sobiet Foreign Min- 
ister Molotov’s statement at the fi- 
nal meeting of the three-power 
conference on the Marshall Plan 
and excerpts from subsequent 
statements py Brit®h Fo?eign Sec- 
retary Bevin and French Foreign

By Mr. Molotov | 


The Soviet delegation has care- | 
fully examined the proposal sub- | 
mitted by the French delegation | 
on July 1. 

The French draft as well as the | 
previous proposal of the British | 
delegation sets the task of draw- 
ing up an economic program for 
the whole of Europe, even though © 
the majority of European coun- | 
tries are known to have no na- 
tion-wide economic programs of 
their own. With a view to elabo- 
rating such a comprehensive 
European program it is proposed 
to set up a special organization 
charged with assessing the re- 
sources and needs of pean 
countries and even with deter- 
mining the development of the 
main branches of industry of 
these countries and only after 
that with ascertaining the possi- 
bilities of receiving American 
economic aid. : 

Therefore, the question of Amer- 
ican economic aid of which indeed 
nothing definite is yet known has 
now provided an occasion for the 
British and French Governments 
to seek the creation of a new 
organization standing over and 

ve the countries of Europe 
and interfering in their internal 
affairs down to determining the 
line of development to be followed 
by the main branches of industry 
in these countries. Furthermore, 
Great Britain and France to-

When efforts are directed

The first form of cooperation is 
based on the development of po- 
litical and economic relations be- 
states possessing equal 
rights and in that case their 
national sovereignty does not suf- 
fer from foreign interference. 
Such is the democratic basis 
for international cooperation 
which brings nations closer to- 
ther and facilitates the task of 
eir mutual aid. 
There exists, however, a differ- 
ent form of international cooper- 
ation based on the predominant 
position of one or several strong 
powers in relation to other coun- 
tries which slip into the position 
of subordinated countries de- 
prived of their independence. 


French Plan Rejected 


It is perfectly obvious that the 
firet form of cooperation between 
states when they act as parties 
possessing .equal rights is radi- 
cally different from the second 
form of international coopera- 
tion, when this principle is not 
observed. 

The Soviet Government, while 
favoring the development of in- 
ternational ‘collaboration on the 
basis of equal rights and mutual 
respect for the interests of the 
contracting parties, cannot lend 
its assistance to anyone in ar- 
ranging his affairs at the expense 
of other countries of less strength 
or size because this has nothing 
in common with normal coopera- 
tion between states. ; 
athe Soviet Government, consid- 
ering that the Anglo-French plan

com re relations between the 
prices of Europe and hamper. 
their cooperation, rejects this

with national sovereignty.

policy, the Navy is closing out its

as springboards in the westward 
drive to conquer Japan.

Towers, chief of the Navy’s gener- 
al board, is directing surveys of all 
naval installations for the purpose 
of lopping off unessential activities 


and effecting economies in line 
with the Navy’s reduced peacetime 
appropriations.

Canada Shippers 
| Curb Communists 


Montreal, July 2 (4)—Canadian 
Great Lakes ship owners said to- 
day that in the future union offi- 
cials boarding their vessels must 
sign an affidavit that they are not 
members of the Communist party 
and will not attempt to foree Com- 
munist teachings on members of 
crews. 

Company officials said the new 
clauge governing movement of 
union officials aboard their ships 
reads: “I swear that I am not a 
Communist or a Communist agent 
and while on the company’s prop- 
erty or aboard its vessels I will not 
advocate, preach, support or dis- 
seminate verbally or otherwise 
amunist ideas and principles.”

Washington, July 2 (*)— The 
United States, with only 1,500 
Army Air Forces combat planes in| 
operation, will have to dig into 
its mothballed air fleet if a United 
Nations world police force is 
created. 

Airmen said today they assume 
that the 1,500 aircraft would be 
entirely inadequate to provide for 
both regular national defense and 
a contribution to the United Na 
tions force. 

In discussing the possibilities of 
such a force, these experts em- 
phasize the current obstacle aris- 
ing out of Russia’s insistence that 
the ground-sea-air components be 


China Viewed As An Index 
This would haye the effect of

Home Bases Presumed 

The presumption at this stage is 
that the individual air forces would 
be based in home territory until an 
emergency arose, 

In the instance of this country’s 
AAF, some airmen suggested, the 
provision for a United Nations con- 
tribution would probably be made 
by expanding the size of the force 


tions for: United Nations duty if 
and when required. 

Thus a certain number of B-29 
groups, medium bomber and fighter 
outfits might be tagged for United 
Nations duty, although their day- 
by-day operations and training 
would be as elements of the regu- 
lar AAF organization. 

25,000 In Reserve 

While the AAF has but 1,500 
first-line aircraft in operation, it 
has an enormous reserve of stored 
airplanes—ahbout 25,000. of all 
types, including transports. 

However, AAF officials said the 
time* required to return these 
planes to operation would be con- 
siderable. The first aircraft would 
probably require up to _ three 
months and the time for getting 
a reasonable percentage of the 
cocooned fleet back into the air 
might requiré as much as a year 
and a half. 

As an indication of the AAF’s 
current position, it was recalled 
that in a recent training “raid” 
against the east coast the Strategic 
Air Command was able to muster 
only 130 B-29s, although it had 
almost 3,000 superfortresses on 
hand after the war.

$754,000,000: Excess, 
First in 17 Years. 


WASHINGTON, July 2 (AP)— 


A $753,787660 surplus, the first in 
17 years, was 
Federal government for the 1947 


chalked up by the 


fiscal year ended Monday. 
Secretary of the, Treasury Snyder 
announced today that the surplus 
was applied on the national debt, 
helping to reduce it to $258,375,903,- 
293 as of Monday midnight. 
Turning to the subject of taxes, 
Snyder told a news conference: 
“As long as bUsiness, employment 
and national in¢ome continue high, 
we should maintain tax revenues 
at levels that will permit a contin- 
ued reduction in the -public debt.” 
Surplus Set at 754 Million 


The nearly $754,000,000 excess of 
government income over spending 
during the last 12 months was an 
improvement of better than $21,- 
400,000,000 over the 1946 fiscal year. 

The reasons for that improvement 
could be summed up this way: 

1. Revenues, approximating $43,- 
259,000,000 rose a surprising $221,- 
000,000 over fiscal 1946 thanks to a 
$2,385,000,000 increase 


Winds Up Fiscal*Period wit 


ions. 
Le Spending, although aBout $6,- 
700,000,000 above original expecta- 
tions, was $21,200,000,000 less than 
in fiscal 1946. The big reason was 


a $28,600,000,000 drop in Army and 
Navy spending. This was offset 
partly by increases of $3,700,000,000 
in expenditures to aid other nations 
and $3,700,000,000 for veterans. 

: Prospect for 1948 Good 

further improvement is in 
prespect for fiscal 1948 just getting 
under way. President Truman has 
indicated the new fiscal year might 
produce a éurplus of over $4,000,- 
000,000, but the outcome is clouded 
by several uncertainties. 

These include how much Con- 
gress w'll vote for spending, wheth- 
er taxes are reduced, whether the 
business activity holds up, and how 
much aid is given other nations. 

The actua] amount of surplus for 
fiscal 1947 was nearly $500,000,000 
below what President Truman pre- 
dicted last April.

The British and French Gov-

that Europe should take the ini-

a@ program to cover Europe’s re-

A temporary organization needs

a basis we I action. This proposal, 
as public here by the 
French Embassy Information Di-

PREAMBLE 
_ The Conference of the Foreign 

Ministers emphasizes the urgency 

of hastening the reconstruction 

and economic development of 
the European countries suffering 
from the effects of the war. It 
believes that this task would be 
facilitated by the economic aid of 
the United States, as proposed by 
'Gen. George Marshall in his 

speech on June 5, 1947. 

The Conference is of the opin- 
ion that Europe should first help 
itself by developing its own basic 
industries. American assistance 
would be a decisive factor in per- 
mitting Europe to make this ef- 
fort by supplying her with the re- 
sources she will lack until the 
goal is achieved.

covery of the European nations

“Sinister Development” . 
Paris, July 3 (P)—The newspaper 
Paris Presse, a middle of the road, 
pro-Gatlle publication, viewed the 
breakup of the three-power con- 
ference as a sinister development 
and declared that July 2, 1947 
would go down as the most im- 


portant date of contemporary 
history. 
“The bridges are cut and so is the 


world, by the same blow,” the paper 
said. “From now on the economic 
and political struggle between the 
two blocs is underway.” — 

The Paris Communist paper Ce 
Soir commented: “The conference 
of the three degenerates into a 
Bevin-Bidault dialogue. Will our 
diplomacy steer toward a new 
Munich?”

and Paul oberts, both of New

mately $2,000 more for legal serv- 
ices for soldiers convicted in a

MESSAGE TO CONGRESS 
The President’s message to Con- 


To the Congress of the United 


States: 


i 


Congress 
' Government to approve the trus- 


I wish to recommend to the 
action enabling this 


teeship agreement for the terri- 
tory of the Pacific islands which 
was approved unanimously by the 
Security Council of the United 
Nations on April 2, 1947. There 
is attached a letter from the Sec- 
retary of State enclosing a copy 
of the trusteeship agreement and 
memorandum with reference to 
its negotiation in the Security 
Council. 

The trusteeship agreement was 
proposed by the United States to 


the Security Council and approved 


by the Council with certain 
changes which were acceptable to 


™ the United States Government. 


Its terms are in conformity with 


the policy of this Government and _ 


with its obligations under the 
Charter of the United Nations. 
The terms of the agreement make 


economic, social and educational 
development of the inhabitants of 
the trust territory, and at the 
same time fully protect the secu- 
rity interests of the United States. 

The United States has taken an 
active role from the beginning in 
the establishment of the trustee- 
ship system of the United Na- 
tions. I believe, therefore, that it 


| would be only fitting, as well as 


in the interest of the inhabitants 


W) of the islands, that the trustee- 


ship agreement should be brought 
into force as soon as possible. 


I have given special considera- | 


tion to whether the attached trus- 
teeship agreement should be sub- 
mitted to the Congress for action 
by a joint resolution or by the. 
treaty process. I am satisfied 
that either method is constitution- 
ally permissible and that the 
agreement resulting will be of the 
same effect internationally and 
under the supremacy clause of 
the Constitution whether advised 
and consented to by the Senate 
or whether approval is authorized 
by a joint resolution. The inter- 
est of both Houses of Congress 
in the execution of this agree- 
ment is such, however, that I 
think it would be appropriate for 
the Congress, in this instance, to 
take action by a joint resolution 
in authorizing this Government 
bs ae the agreement into ef- 
ec 

I hope that the Congress may 
give early consideration to this

The 72-year-old former Demo- 
cratic congressman from Kentucky } 
was accused of accepting more than | 
$50,000 in bribes for getting War &gt; 
Department favors for the Garsson 
brothers’ $70,000, munitions em-

Out 1 Hour, 50 Minutes 

A Federal jury that heard eleven 
weeks’ of testimony deliberated 
only 1 hour and 50 minutes before 
returning its verdict. The maximum 
penalty for each defendant would 


be six years’ imprisonment and 
$30,000 fine. 

Jury Foreman George E. Wells 
solemnly intoned “guilty”*to each 
of the three counts of the indict- 
ment charging that May and the 
Garssons conspired to defraud the 
Government. 

Then, in response to a defense 
request, all seven men and five 
women jurors were polled. Each 
answered “guilty” to all .charges 
against the defendants. ; 

Charles J. Margiotti, head of the 
defense counsel, said he would ap- 
peal within five days.

At that. time, he: told the’ court.” 


“I’m still not guilty!” His Pro 
Henry declined to make any com- 


ment. 

Fourth Defendant Freed | tue 
A fourth defendant, Joseph F. ue 
Freeman, Washington agent for the 
$70,000,000 Garsson munitions 
combine, won a bench-directed ac 
quittal midway in the trial. s 

May and the Garssons denied. 
Government contentions that they- 
conspired to defraud the public 
May’s services in Congress by: 
using his prestige in behalf of the 
Garssons. 

The defense conceded that May~ 
got the money from the Garssons 
but claimed he repaid it by spend- 
ing it all on a Kentucky firm, the 
Cumberland Lumber Company, 
owned by the munitions men.. 

The prosecution asserted that 
the real purpose behind Cumber- 
land was to conceal the alleged 
bribes and set May up in a lucra-” 
tive lumber business. 

The present case grew out of a 
Senate War Investigating Commit- 
tee probe last summer, presided 
over by then Senator James M. 
Mead (D., N.Y.). 

It was brought out in the Senate 
hearings that the Garssons got 
their first war contract on a bor- 
rowed letterhead and ran it into a 
giant arms combine.

The standard phrase used by 
iters of Jefferson’s day to de- 
iscribe man’s essential rights was 
“life, liberty and property.” But: 
to Jefferson, human rights were: 
more important than property 
rights, and the phrase, as he wrote 
it in the Declaration of Independ- 
ence, became “life, liberty and the 
pursuit of happiness.” 


Struggle For Democracy 
The laws and the traditions of} 
the colonies in 1776 were designed 
to support ‘a monarchial system 
rather than a democratic society. 
To Thomas Jefferson the American, 
revolution was far more than a 
struggle for independence. It was# ; 
a struggle for democracy. |kept in isolation. 

Within a few weeks after inde 
pendence had been proclaimed at} 
Philadelphia, Jefferson resigned} 
his seat in the Continental Con- 
gress and returned to his place in 
the Virginia Legislature. There he 
began his monumental work of lay- 
ing the foundation of an independ- 
ent democracy. ... 

Jefferson knew that it was neces- 
sary to provide in law the requi- 
sites for the survival of an inde- 
pendent democracy. He knew that 
it was not enough merely to set 
forth a Declaration of Independ- 
ence. 

Two years ago the United States 
and fifty. other nations joined in 
signing that great declaration of 
yor known as_ the 
Charter of the United Nations. We 
did so because we had learned, at 
staggering cost, that the nations} 
of the world cannot live in ,.peace 
and prosperity if, at the same time, 
they try to live in isolation. 

We have learned that nations 
are interdependent, and that recog- 
nition of our dependence upon one 
another is essential to life, liberty

ommon goals of peace. Of course; 
we cannot expect all nations, with 
different histories, institutions and 
egonomic conditions, to agree at 
ohce upon common ideals and poli- 
cies. But it is not too much to 
expect that all nations should cre- 
ate, each within its own borders, 
the requisites for the growth of 
world-wide harmony. —. 
The first requisite, of peace 
among nations is common ad- 
iherence to the principle that goy- 
ernments derive their just powers 
from the consent of the governed. 
There must be genuine effort to 
translate that principle into reality.

MANILA, Saturday, July 5 —

a remnant of the im Jap-

During the observance of the 
American and Philippine Inde- 
pendence Day, the Japanese sol- 
dier—long-haired and in tattered 
ciothes—marched onto the field 
with a white flag and announced 
he wanted to surrender.

ment said Arukitchi, alone and 
unarmed, had lived in central 
Luzon for two years on fruit 
and wild game after the U. S. 
40th Division wiped out his unit 
in the spring of 1945.

Six Points Outlined 

The proposed loyalty board; in 
determining whether an employé 
or applicant for a Federal job 
should be in Government service, 
would be instructed to consider the 
individual’s record on these six 
points: 

1. Sabotage, espionage, or at- 
tempts or preparations therefore, 
or knowingly associating with spies 
or saboteurs, 
_ 2. Treason or sedition or ad- 
| vocacy thereof, 

3. Advocacy of revolution by 
force or violence to alter the con- 
stitutional form of Government of 
the United States. 

_ 4, Intentional, unauthorized dis- 
closure to any person, under cir- 
cumstances which may indicate dis- 
loyalty to the United States, of doc- 
uments or information of a confi- 
dential or nonpublic character ob- 
tained by the employé making the 
disclosure as a result of his employ- 
ment in or under the executive 
branch of the Government. 

As To Other Governments 

5. Performing or attempting to 
perform his duties as an employé’ 
or otherwise acting, so as to serve 
the interests of another govern- 
ment in preference to the interests 
of the United States. 

6. Membership iin, affiliation 
with, or sympathetic association 
with any foreign or domestic or- 
ganization, association, movement; 
group, or combination of persons 
designated by the attorney gen- 
eral as totalitarian; Fascist, Com- 
munist, or subversive, or as having 
adopted a policy of advocating or 
approving the commission of acts 
of force or violence to deny other 
persons their rights under the Con- 
stitution of the United States, or 
as seeking to alter the form of goy- 
ernment of the United States by 
unconstitutional means.

Spain Sends Protest 


On Aid. Declaration 
MADRID, July 5 (4).—Educa- 


tion Minister 
said today the Spanish - 
ment had protested to the British 
Foreign Office against “mixing the 
Namie of Spain” in the recent 
three-power Paris conference on 
the Marshall proposal for aiding 
Europe. 

The communique issued by the 
British and French Foreign Min- 
isters Thursday said that “all 
European states, with the pro- 
visional exception of Spain,” had 
been invited to participate in re- 
plying to Secretary of State George 
C. Marshall’s suggestions. A French 
Foreign Ministry spokesman said 
the phrase meant that Spain 
would be excluded “as long 
Spain has her present form of gov- 
ernment.” 


The Spanish Education Minis- 
er, reporting on ldst night’s. Cab- 
inet: meeting, told a news confer- 
nce that the “foreign minister 
reported to the Cabinet the failure 
of the Paris conversations for ap- 
Plication of the Marshall plan for 
Europe and on impertinent allu- 
ions made there concerning 
a hypothetical participation of 
Spain.” 

“The Cabinet decided to present 
an energetic protest note to .the 
(British) Foreign Office against 
the unusual act of mixing the 
name of Spain in matters in which 
our country was not asked to in 
tervene,” he said.

Statement by the President. 


The Cabinet Committee on 
World Food Programs, which I 


appointed last September to co-. 


ordinate the activities of the 


Situation at the close of the 
1946-’47 marketing year. They 
show that the American people

We cannot yet ease up our ef-

the world’s urgent post-war 
needs for food. Many millions 
of people are still desperately 


The Cabinet committee re- 
ports that crop prospects abroad 
have been reduced by the severe 
winter in northern Europe, and 
that in the months ahead sub- 
stantial shipments of food— 
especially wheat—must be con- | 


forts to make the maximum | 


possible contribution to world 
needs. There is no room for 
complacency in the general 
situation. 

Food grain, because it is easily 
shipped and stored and because 
it has high food value in rela- 
tion to cost, was the backbone 
of the 1946-’47 export program, 
as it Was a year ago. Cereals, 
including rice, made up slightly 
more than 15,000,000 long tons 
of the total shipments. Wheat,

Can’t Take “Luxury” Goods | 
The quantities of other food- + 
stuffs which can be exporied 
will depend not only upon sup- | 
plies, but also upon their avail- 
ability at relative costs which 
will make them practical im- | 
port commodities for those coun- 
tries and agencies responsible 
for stretching available funds 


needs of hungry people. They 
cannot be expected to take “lux- 


While we continue the neces- 


of foodstuffs, it is very impor- 
tant that we make every effort 
to help the devastated countries 
“help themselves.” The sooner 
these countries get back to their 
normal food production the 
sooner will we be relieved of spe- 


supporting economic units able 
to take their place in a more 


A good illustration of this'sort 
of indir “food” help is the 
program ted by the Army 


cupied zones of Burope. During 
the calendar year 1947 the Army 
plans to supply fertilizer mate- 
rial containing about 160,000 
short tons (143,000 long tons) 
of badly needed nitrogen. This. 
nitrogen is being produced in 
plants which are under Army 
jurisdiction and does not come 
out of our commercially pro- 
duced supplies. It will be a vital 
contribution to the job of get- 
ting these areas back into nor- 
mal domestic food production. 


In addition to the fertilizer 
‘shipments to occupation zones 


crop production. 
Self-Help Program Urged 


More work of the kind which 
will help restore production in 
the needy areas should be done 
in order to reduce the unusual 
drain on American food and 
financial resources. 

The need for devastated coun-. 
tries to get back into normal 
production as soon as possible, 
and to make the most effective 
use of their own supplies, is un- 
derscored by the probability 
that even the utmost efforts of 
the United States and other ex- 
porting countries will again fall 
short of making up all the acute 
food deficits in many countries 
during the year ahead. To this 
end the Food and Agriculture 
Organization, acting behalf 
of the International Emergency 
Food Council, and after a formal 
recommendation by the United 
States Department of Agricul- 
ture, has called a special cereals 
conference in Paris, beginning 
July 9. The effort will be to ac- 
quaint all countries with facts 
of the world food situation 
ahead and to encourage the 
most adequate possible steps on 
the part of importing countries 
to increase the effectiveness of 
their own production, distribu- 
tion! and utilization’ of food 
supplies. 

A summary ofthe more im- 
portant commodity export pro- 
grams and a table giving pre- 
liminary estimates of all food 
shipments for the year are at- 
tached at the end of this report.

Fats and Oils 


Production of edible fats and 
oils in the United States in 1946 
was the smallest since 1940, while 
imports were the smallest since 
1921. The difficult supply situa- 
tion that resulted was the princi- 
pal reason exports of fats and 
oils declined from 337,000 long 
tons in 1945-46 to 233,000 long 
tons in 1946-47.

than 3,000 veterans’ of World War

cational provisions of the GI’ bill, 
the Veterans Administration said 
today.

the list with 1,411, most of them 


Filipinos who served with the 


United States armed forces, Can- 


ada is second with 571. 


The United Kingdom, with 217; 


France, with 175, and Switzerland, 
with 141, have the bulk of 662 stu- 


dents studying in thirteen Euro-| 


pean countries. The’ number in 
other nations there includes Bel- 
gium, five; Czechoslovakia, three; 
Denmark, three; Eire, nineteen; 
Italy, 35; the Netherlands, five; 
Sweden, 54; Spain, one; Greece, 
two, and Norway, two.

Washington, July 5 @) — 
Atomic Energy Commission was 
told today by ‘a board of eminent 
American scientists that there is 
an “urgent and extensive” need 
for further research on the effects 
of atomic energy radiations on 
human life in peacetime and war. 

The board of seven research- 
ers — especially appointed by the 
commission — declared in a report 
made public by America’s atomic 
energy chief, David E. Lilienthal: 

“Because the Atomic Energy 
Commission is charged by law with 
the exclusive control of materials, 
equipment, processes and informa- 
tion which are unique, constantly 
dangerous and certainly not yet 
sufficiently understood, the com- 
mission has every reason to assume 
extensive responsibilities for fur- 
ther development and study of the 
effects of products of atomic fis- 
sion on human ‘life.”

Attitude Is Cautious 

A cautious attitude marked both 
official and scientific comments, 
but Capt. Tom Brown, of the Air 
Forces public relations staff in 

ashington, acknowledged that the 
Air Forces had decided “there's

Calcutta Riots Kill 
28 And _Injure 141 


Calcutta, July 8 (#)—Continued 
Hindu-Moslem...rioting claimed 
three max@elives today, bringing 
the official toll of casualties since 
early yesterday to and 
more than 141 injured. £ 

Unofficia?’réports of the casual- 
ties ran as high as 50 dead and 
more than 200 hurt. “~~ 

Police and the military finally 
brought the situation under con- 
trol after using tear gas and firing 
into the millifig rioters. 

Trams and busses ceased operat- 
ing on most routes while the riot 
was on, and many office workers 
stayed away from work to avoid 
passing through streets.

"LAKE. SUCCESS, July 8—(AP), 
Russia late today charged that the 
situation in Greece was the result 
of American and British interfer- 
ence and demanded that the Uni- 
ted Nations order foreign military 
personnel off Greek soil. ee 

The Soviet Union also called for 
U.N. supervision of all economj 
aid to Greece in a renewed attempt 
to place the American program of 
direct support under international 
control, 

“Direct intervention through the 
presence of foreign troops has been 
supplemented lately by new forms: 


jthe interests of 


so-called military 
tors and in supplying war equip- 
ment,” Deputy Foreign Minister 
Andrei A. Cromyko said in his new 
attack on the American aid pro 
gram. 
Rejects UN Report i 


Rejecting a U.N. report blaming 
Soviet Balkan satellites for the 
Greek border disorders, Gromyko 
Said the Greek government alone: 
was at fault. 

Gromyko put forward the Rus- 
sian rebuttal to a majority report 
of a Balkan investigating commis- 
sion in a 78-minute Speech, one of 
the longest ever delivered to the 
Security Council. 


He asked the council to reverse 
on-the-spot findings and _ rule 
Greece guilty of provoking distur- 
bances with Yugoslavia, Albania 
and Bulgaria. _

frontiers. American Delegate War-

watch would golve the problem and 
Gromyko thus gave the strongest

project.

tish with the 
training groups.

Trade Pact Emphasized 

Today's editions had buried 
stories of the Paris talks\and dis- 
played leading articles on the 
Czech delegation’s hope of obtain- 
ing still stronger trade agreements 
with Russia. 

The French Foreign Ministry 
said in Paris that refusals had been 
received from six nations, all of 
them within the Russian sphere. 
They were Poland, Hungary, 
Romania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and 
Albania. 

Formal acceptances previously 
had been received from fifteen 
states—Austria, Belgium, Den- 
mark, Greece, Eire, Iceland, Italy, 


Luxembourg, Norway, the Nether- 
lands, Portugal, Sweden, Switzer- 


land, Turkey and Czechoslovakia. 

Twenty-two. were invited by 
France and Britain: 

Dispatches from Paris said 
France severely criticized Poland 
and other eastern European na- 
tions for standing aside from con- 
tinental economic co-operation.

general of Pakistan, the new Mos- 
lem state to be created in India.

the present and last viceroy of 
India, will become governor general 
of the Dominion of [India—the name 
by which the separate Hindu state 
of Hindu&amp;Stan will be known.

The Mexican~government announ-

the importation of luxury and non-

dwindling dollar balance in the 
United States. 


The restrictions will go into 


fect tomorrow. 


Beteta, who said Mexico’s dollar 
batarnee in the United States at

would be prohibited. 

Among prohibited items will. be 

furniture, washing machines, rugs, 
automobiles, pianos, watches and 
radios. 
In another list, containing 16 
atezories, the import duties will 
be raised to the 1942 levels, which 
ill make it difficult for import- 
rs to bring in goods. 

The restrictive measures will be 
temporary, Beteta said, but will be 
maintained until Mexico feels her 
conomic position is sound. 

The United States, he said, has 
been notified of the restrictions 
as provided under article 10 of the 
1942 trade treaty.

explosion.

critical masses would have to be 
brought together, a matter “easier 
said than done.”

UNITED NATIONS BY A SYSTEM OF WORLD LAW.”

DATE," SAID A RESOLUTION ON NATIONAL SECURITY ADOPTED AS THE NEA WOUND 
UP A FIVE-DAY CONVENTION. 
THE RESOLUTION ALSO SAID: 
"THE NATIONAL EDUCATION ASSOCIATION RECOGNIZES THAT WE LIVE IN A 
WORLD IN WHICH THE STRUCTURES DESIGNED TO PROVIDE PEACE HAVE YET TO BE 
COMPLETED. TO BE SECURE IN SUCH A WORLD, WE MUST BE STRONG. THE 
NEA IS CONVINCED, THEREFORE, THAT THE AMERICAN PEOPLE MUST AT THIS 
TIME BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THEIR OWN SECURITY, AND CALLS UPON CONGRESS 
TO ENACT SUCH LEGISLATION AS MAY BE REQUIRED TO PROVIDE AN ADPQUATE

Bidault’s Address 


For the first time since the 
end of World War II nations 
which history parted before re- 
uniting them again are gathered 
in a common will of mutual and 
peaceful help. I am happy that 
Paris has been chosen as the 
place of the meeting, which, out 
of the solidarity of unhappiness, 
must create for everybody's 
sake the assertion of a brotherly 
will. 


It is not the fault of any one 


ot us that all the European na-— 


tions are not represented at this 
meeting. Everything that was 
in our power has been done to 
obtain a favorable answer from 
@ unanimous Europe to the ap- 


the thought that has constantly 
inspired us, we will take care 
not to say or do anything that 
would set aside any nation. We 
still hope that seats, empty 
today, will be occupied some 
day. This seems to us, without 
any doubt, in conformity with 
the collective interest of Europe, 
as well as with the’ particular 
interest of every one of the ab- 
sentees. 

We are today fading a task 
whose amplitude and urgency 
are evident to any honest mind. 

Following a terrible ordeal 
which repeated in the same gen- 
eration the first universal disas- 


ter that. struck humanity, Eu- ‘ 


of State. Faithful to 


rope, our con ent, cradle of 
modern civilization, is weakened 
and ravished. A gré€at states- 
man, Mr, Marshall, addressed 
to Europe on June 5 an appeal 
which we want to answer in such 
a way that Europe’s mutual self- 
aid will create conditions for 
temporary but indispensable 
American aid to the Continent. 

It is obviously unnecessary to 
recall today the events since 
General Marshall’s offer and un- 
til the Anglo-Franco-Soviet talks 
in Paris ended the way you 
know. The documents have al- 
ready been published. Any one 
may draw his conclusions after 
studying them, learn what has 
been done for the sake of con- 
ciliation and by whom, what was 
the obstacle to this conciliation, 
and how. 


It has been alleged with a cer- 
tain tendency toward uniform- 
ity, in a bold assertion which I 
notice without wishing to. ex- 
plain it, that this conference was 
a menace not only to the sover- 


eignty of nations, but also to 


their independence. In opposi- 


tion to this charge, whose in- 


sistence does not compensate for 


its inexactness, the sovereignty | 


and the independence of the na- 
tions are here, today, being 
affirmed. - 

What is the object of this 
present conference? Simply to 
establish an organization which 


can tally the balance sheet of 


Europe’s resources and needs, 


It is indispensable that this be 
done quickly. This is the reason 
why:the Franco-British invita- 
tion was handed to you the day 
after the break-up of the three- 
power conference at Paris. This 
is also the reason why such a 
short period Was Jest A an an- 


es is for ow 


swer. 
wili no longer know how to meet 
the purchase of essential goods 
which they are forced to make 
by the current distress of our 
continent without holding corre- 


sponding resources in foreign 
currency. 


Such is the motive for the in- 
itiative taken in common by 
Great Britain and France in the 
mutual interest of Europe, hav- 
ing failed to associate the Soviet 
Union in their invitation. 

We have absolutely no inten- 
tion of imposing views or meth- 
ods, even less to employ this 
conference to establish in Eif- 
rope.a hegemony with which you 
know, gentlemen, that you are 
not here threatened. 


What we are proposing to you 
is to organize, freely and ac- 
cording to what we decide al- 
together, the effort of European 
nations here present so as to 
limit the assistance of the 
United States to strict necessi- 
ties, that is, what we ourselves 


can not do for ourselves by our 
own means, 


It has been aileged that the 


unavowed a aim of our meeting is. 


to rebuild Germany first. The 
resources of Germany ought to 
be utilized for Pr pa Germany 
included. I want’ to emphasize in 
the name of the French delega- 
tion that any other interpreta- 
tion is improper. 

The hour.has come to con- 
struct a Europe, not—as a great 
French voice, that of Aristide 
Briand, proclaimed already 
twenty years ago—not against 
other nations, not against any 
other country or group of coun- 
tries, but for a better disposition 
of the immediate conditions of 
peace to put an end to a state 


of anarchy which gives rise to | 


conflicts by 
tress. 


The whole of Europe is not 
present here, but those who are 
present have the right to speak 
in her name; and to act for her, 

Reinforcements will come, I am 
sure of it, when our loyal work 
will have proved to all, with 
obvious interest, what was the 
path of genuine independence, 

The: hour has come to accom- 
Plish the destiny of Europe by 
returning her to the place which 
was hers, since the deepness of 
the ages, in the life of the civil- 
ized world. 

The noble initiative of the 
government of the United States 
peor ples an appeal 


maintaining dis-— 


Tomorrow, numercus nations 


Soviet Blasts 


betraying them, 

- Together, then, we will make, 

and make it quickly, the effort 

of mutual self-aid which will 

make us worthy of being aided. 
For generations men of all 

countries who rejected a selfish 


} nationalism have longed for this 


assembly which is being held 
today. Let us be proud to be 
witness to it and to be the good 
craftsmen of a task dreamed of 
for centuries and, at the present 
time, urgently necessary. 

I repeat that we did not want 


any refusal, that we spared no 


effort to make our gathering 
more numerous. Such as it is, 
our meeting is a great motif for 
hope for all of us who are here 

and for all those 1 who wi will follow.

London, July 13 (P)—The new} 


cut in newsprint ordered by the 
Chancellor of the Exchequer, Hugh 
D n, carries a grave threat to 
the freedom of the press, Brit- 
ain’s national Sunday newspapers 
charged editorially in unison today. 

They pointed out the effect will 
be to reduce the size of the daily 
newspapers again to four pages— 
they now print six pages three 
times weekly—and the Sunday 
newspapers will drop from eight to 
six pages. The cut is expected to 
go into effect July 21. 

Dalton told the House of Com- 
mons a reduction of 96,000 tons of 
newsprint was necessary to save 
dollars. He estimated the yearly 
saving at between $4,000,000 and 
$8,000,000. 


Annual consumption now is. 420,- 


000 tons. Before 
1,200,000 tons.’ 
The newspapers, however, said 
a saving of $4,000,000 in the next 
six months .would be “out of a 
total trade deficit’of approximately 
500,000,000 pounds ($2,000,000.- 
000) a year,’ and thus would be 
“a trifling sum.” 
“No press is free which has no 
space to say what it wants and 
which lies at the mercy of minis- 
ters who have powers to control 
its size whenever they think it 
worth while to do so,” said the 
Observer. 

No cuts have been announced 
for the weekly journals of opinion, 
including the Economist, the Right- 
wing Spectator, and the Leftist 
Tribune and New Statesman and 
Nation. 4.

Afraid Of Russ Forced Labor

labor in mines or factories.

override President Truman’s prom-

The roll cal] dealt a jolt to the 
Republican leadership. It had been 
predicting hopefully that the tally. 
would foreshadow vi¢tory for their

Forty-eight Republicans and 12 
Democrats, most of them from the 
South, voted for the bill. Republi- 
can Senators Langer of North Dak- 
ota and Morse of Oregon joined 30 
Democrats in opposing the measure.

This directive, issued to you as

as Military Governor in Germany,

ment 

a. Your authority as Military 
Governor will be broadly con- 
etrued and empowers you to take 
action consistent with relevant in- 
ternational agreements, general 
foreign policies of this Govern- 
ment and with this directive, ap- 
propriate or desirable to attain 
your Government’s objectives in 
Germany or to meet military 
exigencies. 

b. Pending arrangements for the 
effective treatment of Germany 
as an economic and political unit, 
you will exert every effort to 
achieve economic unity with other 
zones.

5. United States Political Objec © 
tives in Germany | 


It is an objective of the United 
States Government that there 
should arise in Germany as rap- 
idly as possible a form of political 
organization and a manner of 
political life which, resting on a, 
substantial basis of economic 
well-being, will lead to tranquillity 
within Germany and will contrib- 
ute to the spirit of peace among 
nations. 

Your task, therefore, is funda- 
mentally that of helping to lay 
the economic and educational | 
bases of a sound German democ- 


democratic efforts and of prohib- 
iting those activities which would 


§ecarefully defined and 


‘an excessively centralized 


jeopardize genuinely democratic 
developments. 


6. German Self-Government 


a. You will continue to promote 
the development in Germany of 
institutions of popular self-gov- 
ernment and the assumption of — 
direct responsibility by German — 
governmental agencies, assuring 
them legislative, judicial and ex- 
ecutive powers..consistent with | 
military’ security and the pur- 
poses of the occupation. 

b. It is the view of your Gov- 


ernment that the niost construc- | 


tive “development of German 


political life would be in the es- 


}tablishment throughout Germany 


of federal German states (Laend- 
er) and the formation of a cen- 
tral German government with 
limited 
powers and functions. All powers 
shall be vested in the Laender ex- 
cept such as are expressly dele- 
gated to the Central Government. 

ec. Your Government does not 
wish to impose its own historical- 
ly developed forms of democracy 
and social organization on Ger- 
many and believes equally firmly 
that no other external forms 
should be imposed. It seeks the 
establishment in Germany of a 
political organization which is de- 
rived from the people and subject 
to their control, which operates 
in accordance with democratic 
electoral procedures and which is 
dedicated to uphold both. the 
basic civil and human rights of 
the individual. It is opposed to 
gov- 
ernment which through a concen- 
tration of power may threaten 
both the existence-of democracy 
in Germany and the security of 
Germany’s neighbors and the rest 
of the world. Your Government 
believes finally that, within the 


principles stated above, the ulti- 


mate constitutional form of Ger- 
man political life should be left 
to the decision of the German 


people made freely in accordance | 


with democratic processes.

16. General Economic Objectives 


The economic objectives of the 
United States Government in Ger- 
many are: 

a. to eliminate industry used 
solely to manufacture and to re- 
duce industry used chiefly to 
support the production of arms, 
ammunition and implements of 
war; 


b. to exact from Germany repa- 


ration for the losses suffered by 

United 

quence of German aggression; 

and 

ec. to encourage the German 
people to rebuild a self-support- 
ing state devoted to peaceful 
purposes, integrated into the 
economy of Europe. 

Although the economic rehabili- 
tation of Germany, within the 
framework of these objectives, is 
the task and responsibility of the 
German people, you should pro- 
vide them general policy guid- 
ance, assist in the development 
of a balanced foreign trade and 
insure that German efforts are 
consi#tent with, and contribute 
to, the fulfillment of your Gov- 
ernment’s objectives. 

16. Economic Disarmament and 

Reparation 

a. Your Government continues 
to desire the general fulfillment 
of the principles of the Potsdam 
Agreement regarding reparation 
and industrial disarmament. 

b. Your Government believes 
that the level of industry even- 
tually agreed upon for Germany 


| as a basis for reparation removals, 


while eliminating excess indus- 
trial capacity which has been 
used by Germany for the pur- 
pose of making war, should not 
permanently limit Germany’s in- 
dustrial capacity. The German 
people after the period of répara- 
tion removals should not be de- 
nied the right, consistent with 
continued disarmement, to de- 
velop their resources for the pur- 
pose of achieving higher stand- 
ards of living. 

ec. Your Government does not 
agree to reparation from Ger- 
many greater than that provided 
by the Potsdam Agreement. Nor 
does your Government agree to 
finance the payment of repara- 
tion by Germany to other United 
Nations by increasing its finan- 
cial outlay in Germany or by 
postponing the achievement of a 


self-sustaining German economy. 


Your Government reaffirms the 
principle that the proceeds of au- 
thorized exports shall be used in 
the first place for the payment 
of authorized imports.

where it has been necessary to 
destroy property under the agree-

SALT LAKE CITY, July 15— 
(AP) The nation’s governors coupl- 
ed tonight support of the Marshall 
plan with moves toward endorse- 
ment of the widespread military 
preparedness program. 


The governors’ conference resolu- 
tions committee is studying four 
national preparedness resolutions. 
One is likely to be submitted to 
the 43 governors in attendance for 
a vote tomorrow. 


Secretary of State Marshall's 
plea here for support of his -pro- 
gram to aid Europe drew a gener- 
ally favorable program from the 
governors, 

Gov. Herbert B. Maw, Utah Dem- 
ocrat, said he will ask the resolu- 
tions committee, of which he is a 
member, to draft and report out a 
resolution formally endorsing, the 
secretary’s program. ® 

Urges Preparedness 


Meanwhile J. Strom Thurmond, 
South Carolina Democrat, told his 
colleagues at a luncheon that the 
United States must begin immedi- 
ately to prepare oh a wide scale for 
any eventuality. 


“One of our great allies in the re- 
cent war has embarked on what ap- 
pears to be a policy of isolation- 
ism,” he said. “One group of Eu- 
ropean nations is meeting in Paris 
in an effort to design plans for re- 
habilitation of war-devastated Eu- 
rope. Another group, under the 
leadership of the Soviet: Union, has 
remained away from the Paris con- 
ference.” 


“This choosing up of sides in Eu- 
rope x x x is following a policy 
that leads to war and not to peace,” 
Thurmond declared. + 


He urged universal military train- 
ing, merger of the armed services, 
legislation providing for total mob- 
ilization in case of war, uniform 
hemispheric defensive training and 
armament, and research “‘to stay 
ahead of the world.” —

plan was reflected in statements by 
a cross-section of the 43 governors

Says Prices Far Ahead of Wages 


Henderson appeared before the 
committee representing the Amer 
icans for Democratic Action (ADA). 

He. said prices have run _ far 
ahead of wages and this “imbal- 
ance” has cuj buying power to the 
danger point. 

Taft, continuing his long-stand- 
ing dispute with Henderson over 
economic principles, questioned 
whether there has been any “real 
reduction” of purchasing power. 


“I suggest there is no imbalance” 


between prices and wages. x x x I 
suggest that on the whole wages 
have gone up more than prices,” 
Taft said. 


The ADA program outlined by 
Henderson calls, among other 
things, for an “orderly scaling 
down” of prices by about 50 per 
cent of the increases since June, 
1946. It also recommends wage in- 
creases wherever the 15-cent-an- 
hour increase .pattern of this year 
has not been put in effect. ~ 

Taft Cites Reversal of Stand 

Taft commented that Henderson. 
when he headed OPA in 1942, said 
wage increases threatened the na- 
tion’s economic stability. 

“Now you recommend that we 


cure the present situation by rais- 
ing wages in order to make up pur- | 


chasing power,” Taft said. 


Henderson argued that prices 
were controlled then, and this re- 


quired wage ceilings as well.

less time than it takes to tell about 


Hit, the house passed by unanimous 
ivoice vote and sent to the senate 
tonight a bill appropriating an ad- 
ditional $35,500,000 for veterans’ 
temporary housing. 

By actual count, passage at the 
end of a weary ten-hour session 
came in less than a minute. The 
bill wae not even read, nor wae it 
explained. It was simply passed. 

Approved this morning by the ap- 
|propriations committee, it would 
| provide for conétruction of an esti- 
mated 8,026 units of housing. The 
new funds supplement $438,°62,818 
appropriated to date for the pro- 
gram of conversion of surplus mil- 
itary and other war housing to tem- 
|porary veterans’ dwelling units. 


The bill carries also provision 
the Reconstruction Finance 
jcorporation to use $38,754,700 of its 
javailable funds for administrative 
expenses during the currerit fiscal

isupply bill came before the house,

House spent seven hours and went 
through seven roll-call votes today 
without breaking its deadlock with 
the Senate over the near-billion 
dollar Agriculture Department ap- 
propriation bill for the fiseal year 
which started July 1. 

It compromised to the extent of 
almost $100,000,000 on soil con- 
servation payments but stood pat 
on other major items in dispute as 
it returned the measure to the Sen- 
ate to see if that body would yield. 

Meat !nspection Fund 

The House refused to go along 
with these Senate amendments to 
the bill originally passed by the 
House in May: 

1. Providing $11,140,000 for Fed- 
eral meat inspection by the Agri- 
culture Department. Instead it in- 
sisted that the meat industry foot 
the bill for inspections by paying 
fees to Federal inspectors. . 

2. Providing $75,000,000 for the 
Federal school lunch program in- 
stead of $45,000,000 voted by the 
House. 

3. Appropriating $20,000,000 for 
farm tenant. loans after the House 
had refused to appropriate any- 
thing. 

The House agreed to Senate 
limitations on the crop insurance 
program for the 1948 crop. 


Compromises On $265,000,000 

It compromised the soil conser- 
vation controversy after a long and 
bitter struggle, finally agreeing to 
provide $265,000,000 for this pur- 
pose instead of the $295,000,000 
demanded by the Senate and the 
$165,614,290 originally voted by the 
House. 

But the House refused to accept 
a Senate amendment authorizing 
the obligation of $150,000,000 for 
conservation payments for the 
1948 program and applied to this 
year’s program a limit of $500 that 
may be paid to any individual. The 
Senate had voted that limitation on 
the 1948 program only.

FRENCH VIEW 


Ambassador Says Deci- 
‘sion Now Would Im- 


July 18 (P)—France 
served notice through her Ambas- 
sador today that a British-American 
decision now to revive German in- 
dustry might “greatly endanger” 
Europe's efforts to put the Marsha 

aid plan into effect. : 

The envoy, sub- 
mitted the French ment’s 
views in an hour-long conference 
with Robert Lovett, under secre- 
tary, at the State Department. 

Referring plainly to the tentative 
agreement already reached by the 
United States and Britain virtually 
to double the present ceiling on 
western Germany steel production, 
he said afterward that: 

“The Paris conference on the 
Marshall plan is going very well 
and is likely to produce results in’ 
something like six weeks. But if in 
the meantime France is faced with 
decisions she cannot approve, the 
conference could be greatly en- 
dangered.” 

Expense Of Neighbors’ 

He advised particularly that “no 
decision should be made which 
would create a fait accompli” on 
German’s future during the con- 
ference which would be “at the ex- 


was not opposing such a meeting, 
“We're all out for digging the 
coal,” he said, “but not for using it 


in Germany to make German 
steel.” 
Called ‘Battle Of Ruhr’ 

The French statement added con- 
fusion to an already involved situ- 
tion over German production which 
a London official termed today the 
“Battle of the Ruhr.” Developments.

‘Gray Mart’ 
In Newsprint 


New York, July 18 (#)—Some 
United pete 
Hers are paying sky-hig ices for 
newsprint in an international free 
market that stretches from New 
York to the Orient. 
Paper from Canada, Sweden, 
France and Poland is being sold 
and offered at prices from around 
$200 a ton up—with the accent on 
the “up.” At least one publisher 
has paid $290 a ton. voo8 
This $290 charge is 219 per cent 
above the so-called contract price 
of $91 a ton delivered in New York, 
the price at which the great bulk of 
newsprint, mostly from-Canada, is 
sold in the United States; 
Publishers of metropolitan dai- 
lies as well as small-town papers 
are paying fancy prices to pad out 
dangerously low supplies. News- 
print stocks held by all United 
States publishers at the end of May 
were at the lowest level on record 
and only slightly higher at the end 
of June, according to the latest 
report of the American Newspaper 
ers Association. ..

Bevin Hopes To Br U.S. 
And Russia 


Morpeth, England, July 19 


Ernest Bevin, Foreign Secretary, | 
said today tn saw no danger of an- 


other war “‘in generation,” 
and expressed the hope that Brit- 
ain would find a way to “unite the 


United States and Russia in a 


common endeavor for the uplift of 
humanity as a whole.” 

Speaking extemporaneously at a 
coal miners’ picnic in this northern 
England town, Bevin took a sober 
view of Britain’s eeonomic diffi- 


ma culties, He said the British policy 


would be to keep dollar-borrowing 
to a minimum. ~ 

“It is very hard to negotiate with 
the people to whom you are: in 
debt,” he added. “When you can- 
not pay up they feel a bit superior.” 


Signs Of Deep Conviction . 


The Secretary spoke with signs 
of deep conviction as he said “there 


mis no danger of another war in this 


eneration, as far as I can see. 
“But in every act you perform, 


Sayou must. keep in mind the chil- 
oa dren of 30 ov 40 years from now. 


“Not a day passes—not a mo- 
ment passes—in the job in which 
I am now engaged without my be- 
ing fully conscious that a wrong 
decision, wrong judgment or petu- 
lant answer may now condemn a 
generation.” 

Bevin referred several times to 
the role of the United States in 
the world of the future. 

Cites Marshall Stand 

“I hope that the United States 
will never withdraw from Europe 
again,” he said. 

Bevin said Gen. George C. Mar- 
shall, Secretary of State, had “laid 
it down” that if Britain wanted 
more money “we must not see how 
much we wanted, but how little.” 

“Tl think that is a sound basis 
and I am going to try it,” he added, 

The Secretary addressed a fre- 
assuring word to France about 
Germany's future strength. 

“I have seen it said in the press 
that the work | ,haye been doing 
at Paris (at thed'sixteen-nation 
economic conference) in trying to 
take advantage of the Marshall 
proposals is intended to recreate 
Germany. It is nothing of the kind, 
German restoration must take its 
place in the queue of the general 
economic recuperation of Europe.

on us?’

look at our security. We cann 
face another Germany of that kind, 
and we are not going to. ere

tained. At what point is security 
safe, and at what level can we allow 
German production to be main- 
tained?”

British Explain 


Loan ‘Draws’ 


London, July 19 (®)—A Treasury 


spokesman said today the sudden} 


new withdrawals from Britain’s 


§ dollar loan in Washington were due 


“partly” to the Anglo-American 
currency convertibility agreement 
which went into effect Tuesday. 

Under the agreement, which is 
one of the terms of the loan itself, 
nations to which Britain becomes 
indebted through current trading 
may demand dollars as payment. 
Several nations, with which Britain 
signed separate agreements, also 
may demand dollars in payment 
for the small released portions of 
debts which Britain piled up dur- 
ing the war. 


_ Heavy Run Doubted 

British officials had insisted in 
recent months they expected no 
unduly heavy run by creditor na- 
tions on Britain’s dollar resources 
— the agreement became effec- 

ve. 

Spokesman said today that it is 
“utterly impossible” to say yet ex- 
actly how much the money with- 
drawn recently from loan would be 
used for payments to other nations. 

“Lot Of Bits Due” 

Stepping up the rate of with- 
drawals, Britain took $150,000,000 
shortly before the convertibility 
date, another $100,000,000 on the 
date itself, and another $150,000,- 
000 yesterday. 

Treasury spokesmen said one 
reason was that “a lot of bills seem 
to be coming due at this time.” 

Other authoritative Whitehall in- 
formants suggested price rises in 
America and heavy expenditures in 
the British zone of Germany may 
have been contributing

Uurges Some Wage Rises 


In some cases wage increases 


-are still needed to attain work- 


able relations in the wage and 
salary structure, and to alle- 
viate hardship to wages 
which are substandard or which 
have risen substantially less 
than the increase in the cost of 
living. 

Except for such special cir- 
cumstances, wage increases 
should be related to general 
trends in productivity and not 
made on a basis which forces 
price increases or prevents price 
reductions needed to assure sale 
of increasing supplies. 

._ With the wage adjustments 
already made and those still 
needed in special wage areas, it 
follows that the patterns of 
workable price relations ulti- 
mately arrived at will be on a 
somewhat higher price level 
than would otherwise have come 
about. However, this is not a 
justification for pyramiding 
wage-price increases or failing 
to make price reductions when- 
ever and wherever possible. 


In the interest of those whose 


income has remained substan- 


, dard, it is imperative that legis- 


lation be enacted to extend the 


| coverage of the fair labor stand- 


ards act, to increase the mini 
mum wage level to at least 
cents an hour, and to enlarge 


| social-security: benefit: payments 


in view of the higher cost of

Recommends Caution 

Similarly, increases in the. 
pricé of steel would have a wide- 
spread inflationary effect. Steel 
companies should exercise .ex- 
traordinary caution at this stage | 
of our reconversion effort to see 
that increases in coal prices or 
other costs are offset as fully as 
possible through the savings of 
continuous and high-level opera- 
tion. Recent favorable earnings 
should permit the absorption of 
an extraordinary cost over a 
short period in order to stabilize 
prosperity for the longer run. 

In no case should the particu- 
lar wage increases in the mining 
industry be made the basis for 
wage demands in other fields 
governed by different circum- 
stances. 

It is in the interest of steady 
expansion of the economy that, 
with the aid of collective bar+ 
gaining, prices and wages be 
brought in line with general pro- 
ductivity trends.

themselves. 

Relations of all three with the

WASHINGTON, July 22. — (AP) 
The house voted today to strip tne 


administration of all guthority to 
control installment buying. The 


measure oses to end immed- 


chases of such things as automo- 
biles, refrigerators and radios. 


The senate had approved a bill 
to continue the controls in modi- 
fied form to December 31 but the 
house rejected this and. sent its. 
own measure to the senate. 

Since President Truman has ad- 
vised congress he will lift the con- 
trols imposed in wartime—unless 
congress gives him peacetime au- 
thority—today’s house action point- 
ed directly toward an early end of 
all installment buying regulations. 

Brush Aside Truman Request + 


The house action was by voice 
vote. There was no rollcall. 

The house vote brushed aside Mr. 
Truman’s request that he be given 
peacetime authority to. continue the 
installment . buying curbs, as 4/| 
check against inflationary tenden- 
cies. The controls (known as Re- 
gulation W), were instituted by ex- 
ecutive order under authority of 
the trading with the enemy act. 

They require one-third down 
payments, with installments run- 


ent by Rep. M 


year and another by Rep. Buffett 


mobile credit purchases. 


ed “to remove these controls at this 


ning no more than 15 months, on 
automobiles, cooking. stoves and 
ranges, mechanical , dishwashers, 
ironers, refrigerators, washing ma- 
chines, room unit air conditioners, 
radios, phonographs, sewing ma- 
chines and suction cleaners. 

A 20 per cent down payment, 
installments limited to 15 
months, is required for furniture 
and soft surface floor coverings. 

The bill approved by the senate 
would extend the controls to De- 
cember 31, with the down payment 
required to be no more than 20 per 
cent, and the installments to be 
limited to two years. 

In a report preceding the house 
vote, a majority of the house bank- 
ing committee said Regulation W 
“bears most heavily on persons of 
limited income and in many cases

them from these markets.”

hands-off policy toward the Indon-

that American arms used by the 
Dutch forces were supplied almost 
entirely in wartime to fight the 
Axis. 
Since V-J day, he told a news 
conference, the United St&amp;tes has 
neither supplied arms for) Ose in 
Indonésia nor.transported them ex-

a Dutch marine brigade of 4,800 
men trained in this country during 
the war. 

A few weeks after V-J day, the 
State department turned down the 
Netherland’s request for permission 
to ship arms to Indonesia via the 
United States. It also barred the 
use of American vessels for Car- 
rying Dutch troops to the East In- 
dies colonies.

JAPANESE INVADERS.

mBUT AT PRESENT WILL NOT INCLUDE SINGAPORE WHERE 380,000 OF THE 
MAREA'S MALAYA'S 5,000,000 PEOPLE LIVE.

and British zones, evoked some dis-

Surprised By Action 

Officials here were surprised by 
the State action. 
They had not been informed of the 
Marshall letter to Georges Bidault, 
French Foreign Minister, replying 
to French protests against a Brit- 
ish-American agreement in Berlin 
-to raise-the level of German indus- 
try to between 10,000,000 and 12,-) 
000,006 tons of steel annually. The 
French said revival of German in- 
dustry on such a scale was a po- 
tential threat to French security, 
and was a question which should be 
settled by the four-power Foreign 
Ministers Council. 

The Marshall letter was 
ted by the French as an invitation 
to a French-British-American con- 
ference which the French said yes- 
terday they would accept.

Germany the greater of the two

The State’ Department's proposal 
for a new conference on German 
industrial levels, with France in- 
cluded, was a sharp disappointment 
in military government circles 
who fear that new deadlocks and 
delays will result while Germany's 
precarious economy crumbles. 

. “Back At Petsdam” 

“T think now we are right back 
where we were at Potsdam and 
the situation is far more critical,” 
said one top official... “If we are 
going to have a policy let's have 
one and carry it out, and not re- 
verse our field every. five months.” 

“We seem to be trying to ride 
two horses going in different di- 
rections,” he added, 

When the Moscow Conference of 
Foreign Ministers failed to agree 
on uniting Germany this spring, 
largely because the question of 
reparations became entangled with 
other economic problems, the Brit- 
ish and American military authori- 
ties set out upon an export-import 
program for their two zones. 

Headed For Ash Can 

This program involved an in- 
crease in the industrial level and 
had. as its objective the making of 
Germany self-supporting by 1950 
and the lifting of the occupation 
load from the taxpayer at home. 

With the plan at the point of be- 
ing announced, it was held up at 
French request. Military Govern- 
ment officials said they now be- 
lieved it was headed for the ashcan. 

The French Foreign Office view 
expressed yesterday was that any 
three-power conference on Ger- 
man industry would be a “study” 
with no. decisions -contemplated 
until next November’s Foreign 
Ministers’ Conference in London in 
which Russia will participate.

Batavia, Java, July 25 (P)—Quali- 


fied sources said today that forma- 
tion of seven separate states from 
former territories of the Indone- 
sian Republic was a “probability” 
when Dutch troops completed mili- 
tary operations against the Re- 
publicans. 


These informants, discussing 


what might be expected politically 


in the islands, said the Dutch would 
allow separate parts of Republican 
territory to become Federal spart- 
ners in the projected United States 
of Indonesia, if the population so 
desired. 

The United States of Indonesia 

as to include Java, Sumatra and 
Madoera. 

Proposed Alignment 

One source said the linguistic 

and cultural differences among 


the various peoples of Java and 


Sumatra made it probable that the 
federation of separate states wouls 
be chosen. If this were the case 
the informants said, the state 
might. be made up as follows: 


1. Central Java, seat of the 


present Republic, which might 
continue to exist within a federa- 
tion if the Republican leadership 
was willing to co-operate. 

2. West Java, where 12,000,000 
Sundanese speak a language of 
their own. 


3. East Java and the Island of 


Madoera, largely populated. by 4 
Madoerese, with a distinct cul- | 


ture of their own. 

4. Atieh (Achin), in northern 
Sumatra, whose population is 
made up of clannish Moslems. 

5. The Batak country and ithe 
northeast coastal people in su- 
matra, largely Batak Chris ms, 
inhabiting an area beginning 
about 150 milegnorth of Padang 
and running northwest across 
the island as far as Pematang- 
siantar.

around Padang and Fort de

To Take Broad View 

British officials. said today that 
while the Americans still wanted 
the talks to be confined to stepping 
up coal output,.they would be ready 
t. take a broad view of the 
measures necessary to achieve im-

questions other than management, 
equipment and working conditions; 

Authoritative sources said the 
wider problem of the control and 
ownership of the Ruhr mines was 
not on the agenda but it was 
certain to come up. Britain still 
maintains, they said, that socializa- 
tion would give the German miners 
a greater incentive to work. In any 
case, they argued, it was “unthink- 
able” either to return the mines. to 
former Nazi-minded owners or to 
hand them over to private United 
States interests. 

France had made it clear, mean- 
while, that she favors reserving 
decisions on Germany’s industrial 
levels for the Foreign Ministers 
Council next November. . 


If, as a result of these confer- 
ences, a partition of Germany 
emerges, British sources stated 
their conviction that it was likely 
to mean “little else than Europe’s 
partition.”

ment Of Unmatched Strength } 


New York, July 27 (4)—Major 
Alexander P. de Seversky, aircraft 
designer and long-time exponent 
of air power, said today unification 
jof the nation’s armed forces “can 
become an instrument of un- 
matched strength under our demo- 
cratic conditions.” 

“What airmen have fough for 
all their lives has finally become 
a reality,” he said in a statement. 
“Air force has been emancipated 
and put on a basis of equality with 
the Army and Navy.” 

‘ Advantages Can Be Lost 

He said, however, that “the im- 
mense advantages of autonomy for 
the three departments—Army, 
Navy and Air—can easily be lost, 
or even turned into liabilities, if 
the development of any of them is 
cramped by regimentation from 
above.” 

The airman urged that “each de- 
fense component be placed under} 
the most qualified and independent- | 


aged to develop its strategic po- 
tential to the maximum.” Only in 
that way, he added, “can we make 
sure that each of them will make a 
contribution in proportion to its 
true strategic significance.” 

Identical With Nazi Setup 
De Seversky said that “it may 
come as startling news to the aver- 
age layman that our new defense 
setup is essentially identical with 
the one that was in force in Nazi 
Germany,” and pointed out that|} 
“the late Reich had autonomous 
army, navy and air force, headed 
by Hitler as a kind of secretary of 
defense, with a supreme command 
equivalent to our joint chiefs of 
staff.” 

“But there is no cause for alarm 
in the parallel,” he added. “A sys- 
tem that failed dismally under a 
totalitarian regime, with its ex- 
treme of regimenitation, can be- 
come an instrument of unmatche 
strength under our democratic con- 
ditions.”

BROADCAST NEEDS 


WASHINGTON, July 28—(AP) 
Senators and representatives de- 
cided today to make a joint inves- 
tigation of the State Department's 
foreign information service, in- 
cluding “Voice of America” broad- 
casts, and to visit Europe in the 
fall to study its effectiveness. 

The Senate and House separate- 
ly authorized investigations. The 
chairmen of the inquiry commit- 
tees, Senator Smith (R-N.J.) and 
Rep. Mundt (R-S.D.) got together 
today and decided to operate as a 
unit here and overseas. 

Raps Russian Stand

ment saying:

country to be spending billions of 
dollars for the relief of the devas- 


iitated countries of the world, only 


to. have Russia and her satellite 
countries interpret it as this coun- 
try having imperialistic designs.”

congressman who goes abroad this 
summer or fall to *eek information

2-World Concept Is Seen 
Probable by Eisenhower 


By The Associated Press. 

BILLINGS, Mont., July 28— 
Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower said 
today that “it looks more and 
more as though the United States 
will have to accept a two-world 
concept when we have been 
working for a one-world plan.” 

The Army Chief of Staff made 
the statement to a reporter dur- 
ing a refueling stop here on the 
way to Alaska to inspect mili- 
tary posts. , 

He conferred with Tom Camp- 
bell, Hardin, Mont., wheat opera- 
tor, who told him that Big Horn 
County will have the biggest 
wheat crop in history this year. 

General Eisenhower comment- 
ed that “food is the number-one 
step in the Marshall Plan. 

“Food will give Europe the 
chance at the degree of stability | 


needed to work out its problems,” | : 


he said.

Balkan Vote Test 


Lake Success, July 28 (?) — A 
consensus of delegates indicates 
that a far-reaching decision may 
come tomorrow on the Balkan 
problem, and with it a test of the 
United Nations’ powers for effec-

ment of disputes. 

As the United Nations Security

lexpected a vote tomorrow, or not

Serious If Soviet Doesn’t Veto

AVIV RIOT 


Palestinians did not have long to 
wait and tonight, a reliable source 
said, Jews and British soldiers 
clashed in the streets of the aill- 
BJewish city of Tel Aviv and in- 


discriminate NI began from 
armored cars, l 

The raking of tw int 
fire caused most of the casualties, 
the source said. Three persoms were 
killed in one bus and one in an- 
other, while a fifth person died in 
a hospital of bullet- wounds. At one 
time, eight armored cars opened 
up with their guns, the informant 
reported. 

The dead were two women, two 
men and a young boy. Damage to 
shops and other property was 
placed at $100,000. Late tonight all. 
British troops and British police 
patrols were«withdrawn from Tel; 
Aviv and the tension eased. 

In Jerusalem sirens sounded 4 
general alarm at 11:50 p.m., when 
gunfire was heard near the central 
police’ station. The all-clear signal 
was given a few minutes later. 
There were no casualties. 

A Jewish source said that Haga- 
nah, moderate Jewish underground 
group, was fearful of the result of 
the Tel Aviv incident—bloodiest 
single episode in the past weeks’ 
history of Holy Land violence—-and 
ordered its members, which it calls 
the “Jewish National Defense 
Army,” on .a “stand by” basis 


found, hastened to their bases. 
A British civil authority said, 
however, that there was little 
chance that martial law would be 
imposed on the area immediately. 
“There will-be some searches, of§ 
course, and the populace may be 
inconvenienced a bit, but no mili- 
tary control is planned, at least 
for the present,” he said. 

The area was cordoned off and 
dogs were turned loose in an at- 
tempt to pick up the trail of the 
killers,

Seen “Turning Point” . 

Some government foreign trade 
experts privately called the export 
decline “a probable turning point” 
—the beginning of a downtrend in 
a $16,000,000,000-a-year business” 
now furnishing employment for an 
estimated 3,500,000 Americans. 

Others, somewhat more cautious, 

ted that there was a two-day 

ipping strike in June and that 
the month had one less working 
day than May. They said this 
might have accounted for part of 
the drop. 

But all tended toward agreement 
that if June did not mark the turn- 
ing point, July or August almost 
certainly will show the export pro- 
fit sinking. ' 

There was agreement also on the 
causes: 

1. Rapid ghtinking of foreign 
holdings of gold and U. S. dollars, 
the only kinds of money that will 
pay for American goods. 

2. Tightening up by foreign coun- 
tries on their purchases to conserve 
buying power that is fading while 
need for it grows.

WASHINGTON, July 31 — (AP) 
American exports in June slumped 
13 percent below May’s record. 

The census bureau, reporting to- 
day that June shipments were 
$180,000,000 below the May peak of 
$1,422,000,000 called it “the first 
substantial interruption in the re- 
cent rising trend of exports.” ; 


President Truman in an econom-. 
ic report to Congress last Monday, 
had classed the “extraordinary ex-. 
cess of exports over ,imports” as 


inal nine-day notice 


neath the nation’s high employ- 


Commerce Department officials 
estimated foreign holdings of gold 
and dollars had dropped $1,000,000,- 
000 or more during the second quar- 
ter of the year as foreign buying in 
the U. S. ate into this reserve. 

They figured other countries still 
have upwards of $19,000,000,000 in 
gold and dollar assets, but: observ- 
ed that the holdings are unevenly 
distributed so that many countries 
in greatest need of reconstruction 
have little. 

Tighten Up on Buying 

The numLer of countries tighten- 
ing up on buying in the U. S: 
through import restrictions has 
been growing. It now includes Swe- 
den, Mexico and several South Am-~ 
erican countries, with Britain and 
others likely to join the list. 

Simultaneously, the unspent 
amount of U. S. loans that have 
furnished the means for paying 


about half the net debt of other: 


countries on trade with the U. §. 
has shrunk below $4,400,000,000 at 
a rate indicating exhaustion in a 
comparatively few months, 

Hard-pressed Britain, spending 
its $3,750,000,000 loan twice as fast 
as originally expected, has used 
$700,000,000 this- month alone 
has but $1,000,000,000 left — 
amount seemingly sure to be ans 
by the end of the year.

Washington, July 31 (A. P.).— 
President. Truman today wel- 
comed Dr. Eel¢o Van Kleffens to 
his new post as"Dutch Ambassa- 
dor to the United’ States. 

There was no word of refer- 
ence to the fighting in Indonesia 
when the envoy and former For- 
eign Minister presented his let- 
ters of credence at the White 
House. Mr. Truman told.him that 
“the cordial relationship betweert 
our two countries has been of 
very long standing,” and added: 
“The people of the United States! 
not soon forget the gallant 
role played by the people of Hol- 
land during. the war, and have 
viewed with admiration the ef- 
forts and progress toward re: 
construction and recovery in the 
Netherlands. since the war. I can 
assure you, Mr. Ambassador, that 
the officials of the American Gov-' 
ernment are prepared to extend 
to you their full co-operation in 
the fulfillment of your mission.” 

He asked also that the Ambas- 
sador convey to his Sovereign 
Queen Wilhelmina, sincere wishes 
tor her welfare and her country’s. 

Van Kleffens said that his 
country and. the United State 
have a strong bond in common 
“ideals of liberty and of respect 
for the rights of the individual.”

ity Council, “I'll say what I have

The coin bill Mr. Truman vetoed 
would have commemorated the | 
100th anniversary of the admission 
of Wisconsin into the union May 
29, 1948. Mr. Truman said in a 
statement that there are so many 
similar proposals as to cause con- 
fusion. He said it would be “im- 
possible to enact one bill and ignore 
all the others.” 

Commemoretive half dollars in 
the past have been issued to organi- 
zations promoting ceremonies, 
causes, etc., and these in turn have 
raised money by re-selling them at 
a premium price. Some have 
achieved a rarity making them 
worth many times 50 cents. 

Mr. Truman said that too many 
designs on coins “tends to create. 
confusion, to increase the possib- 
ility of counterfeiting, to encourage 
traffic in commemorate coins for 
private profit” and to get away 
from the fundamental. purpose o 
money—a medium of exchange.
